html:
Russian America was Russia's colony in North America, covering most of today's Alaska with outposts as far south as California, from its first permanent settlement in 1784 until the sale of Alaska to the United States in 1867.

After Vitus Bering's voyage of 1741 brought back sea otter pelts, Siberian fur hunters worked their way along the Aleutian Islands. They forced Unangax̂ men to hunt sea otters by holding their families hostage, and violence and disease killed most of the people. In 1784 Grigory Shelikhov founded a settlement at Three Saints Bay on Kodiak, among the Sugpiaq. In 1799 the tsar gave the Russian-American Company a monopoly over the colony.

Its manager Alexander Baranov pushed southeast into Tlingit land. The Tlingit destroyed the fort at Sitka in 1802; the Russians retook the site in 1804, and Sitka, then called New Archangel, became the capital. Fort Ross, founded in 1812 in Kashaya Pomo land north of San Francisco, grew food for the colony until 1841.

Only a few hundred Russians lived there at any time. Orthodox priests baptised many Native people, and Orthodox churches still stand among the Sugpiaq, Unangax̂ and Yup'ik. Once the sea otters were hunted out, the colony lost money, and Russia sold it.
sum: Russian America was Russia's colony in North America, covering most of today's Alaska with outposts as far south as California, from its first permanent settlement in 1784 until the sale of Alaska to the United States in 1867.
